topics.ch: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
topics.t: The French Revolution and the idea of the nation
topics.h: Imagine your whole country deciding: 'We are not the king's subjects any more, we are citizens!' That is what France did in 1789.
p: A nation-state is a state in which most citizens share a sense of common identity and history. Earlier, much of Europe was ruled by dynastic empires that held many different peoples together under one ruling family.
The French Revolution of 1789 transferred sovereignty (supreme power) from the monarch to the body of French citizens.

Revolutionaries spread the ideas of la patrie (the fatherland) and le citoyen (the citizen). The tricolour replaced the royal standard, and the Estates General, elected by active citizens, was renamed the National Assembly.

They set up a centralised administration with uniform laws for all, abolished internal customs duties, brought a uniform system of weights and measures, and made French as spoken and written in Paris the common language.

Napoleon's Civil Code of 1804 (the Napoleonic Code) ended privileges based on birth, made all equal before the law and secured the right to property. But higher taxes, censorship and forced conscription made many conquered people hostile to French rule.

ex.q: Think it through: Why would replacing the royal flag with a new tricolour help turn subjects into a nation?
st: A royal flag stands for one ruling family; the people under it are only subjects.
A tricolour stood for the whole people, not for a king.
When everyone salutes the same new symbol, they feel they belong to one community with shared rights.
So symbols like the flag, new hymns and oaths built a sense of collective identity.
ex.a: The tricolour made people feel that the nation belonged to all citizens, not to the king, which strengthened a shared national identity.

topics.rl: Our own Tiranga, the national anthem and the Republic Day parade are symbols that make crores of Indians feel they belong to one nation.

topics.ch: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
topics.t: Liberals, conservatives and the Treaty of Vienna
topics.h: After Napoleon was defeated, Europe's kings tried to press the rewind button. But new ideas cannot be un-thought!
p: Liberalism comes from the Latin root liber, meaning free. For the new middle classes it meant individual freedom, equality before the law, a constitution, representative government through parliament and the safety of private property.
In revolutionary France, however, the right to vote and to be elected was given only to property-owning men. Women and men without property were left out.
In 1834 a customs union called the Zollverein was formed at the initiative of Prussia. It removed tariff barriers and cut the number of currencies in the German states from over thirty to two.

In 1815 Britain, Russia, Prussia and Austria met at Vienna, hosted by the Austrian Chancellor Duke Metternich. The Treaty of Vienna restored the Bourbon dynasty in France and set up states on France's borders to stop future French expansion.

Conservative regimes used censorship to control newspapers and books. Revolutionaries such as Giuseppe Mazzini, born in Genoa in 1807, formed secret societies: Young Italy in Marseilles and Young Europe in Berne.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did German merchants welcome the Zollverein?
st: Before 1834 goods moving across the German states paid customs duty at many borders.
Each state also had its own currency, weights and measures, so trade was slow and costly.
The Zollverein removed tariff barriers and reduced currencies from over thirty to two.
A single economic territory made trade easier and also strengthened the wish for a united Germany.
ex.a: It removed internal tariffs and cut the number of currencies, making trade cheaper and supporting national unity.

topics.rl: Just as one GST system replaced many separate state taxes so goods can move more easily across Indian states, the Zollverein made trade simpler across the German states.

topics.ch: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
topics.h: Metternich once grumbled, 'When France sneezes, the rest of Europe catches cold.' In 1830 and 1848, France sneezed loudly!
p: In July 1830 liberal revolutionaries in France overthrew the Bourbon kings and set up a constitutional monarchy headed by Louis Philippe. This sparked an uprising in Brussels, and Belgium broke away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.
The Greek war of independence began in 1821. Supported by many West Europeans, it ended with the Treaty of Constantinople of 1832, which recognised Greece as an independent nation.

Romanticism used art, poetry, music and folk culture to create national feeling. The German philosopher Johann Gottfried Herder said true German culture lived among the common people, das volk. In Poland, under Russian rule, using the Polish language became a sign of resistance.

The 1830s brought hardship: population grew, jobs were few and food prices rose. In 1848 food shortages and unemployment in Paris forced Louis Philippe to flee; a Republic was proclaimed and all adult males above 21 got the vote.

Also in 1848, middle-class liberals in the German states met at the Frankfurt Parliament in the Church of St Paul on 18 May 1848. Its 831 elected representatives offered a crown to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, King of Prussia, but he rejected it. Women could only watch from the visitors' gallery.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did the Frankfurt Parliament fail?
st: It was made up mostly of middle-class professionals and lost the support of workers and artisans.
It offered the crown of a united Germany to Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia.
He rejected it and joined other monarchs opposing the elected assembly.
Without royal or military support and with a narrow social base, the assembly was finally disbanded.
ex.a: It had a narrow middle-class base and was opposed by the monarchy and the army, so it was forced to disband.

topics.rl: When the Grimm brothers collected German folk tales, they were doing something like collecting dadi-nani stories from Indian villages: saving the voice of ordinary people as part of national culture.

topics.ch: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
topics.h: Two puzzles, two master builders: Bismarck fitted Germany together with 'blood and iron', while Cavour and Garibaldi assembled Italy piece by piece.
p: After 1848, nationalism moved away from democratic revolution. Conservatives used state power and armies to build nations.

Prussia led German unification. Its chief minister Otto von Bismarck, backed by the Prussian army and bureaucracy, fought three wars over seven years, with Austria, Denmark and France, all won by Prussia.

In January 1871 the Prussian king, William I, was proclaimed German Emperor in a ceremony at the Hall of Mirrors in Versailles. The new state focused on modernising currency, banking, and the legal and judicial systems.

In the mid-19th century Italy was divided into seven states. Only Sardinia-Piedmont was ruled by an Italian princely house; the north was under the Austrian Habsburgs, the centre under the Pope and the south under the Bourbon kings of Spain.

King Victor Emmanuel II and his chief minister Count Cavour led unification. Through a diplomatic alliance with France, Sardinia-Piedmont defeated Austria in 1859. In 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi's volunteers marched into the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and in 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy.

ex.q: Think it through: Mazzini's uprisings of 1831 and 1848 failed. Why did Sardinia-Piedmont succeed later?
st: Mazzini relied on secret societies and revolutionary uprisings without a strong state behind them.
Sardinia-Piedmont was a kingdom with its own army and a skilled chief minister, Cavour.
Cavour made a diplomatic alliance with France, which helped defeat Austria in 1859.
Garibaldi's volunteers then won the south, and the movement came together under King Victor Emmanuel II in 1861.
ex.a: Unification succeeded when a strong state with an army and clever diplomacy took the lead, joined by popular volunteers.

topics.rl: Just as hundreds of princely states had to be brought together into the Indian Union after 1947, Germany and Italy had to join many separate states into one country.

topics.t: War, satyagraha and the Rowlatt Act
topics.h: A thin man in a simple dhoti returned from South Africa with an idea so powerful that an empire did not know how to fight it: the power of truth.
p: The First World War created hardship in India: defence spending rose, taxes and customs duties went up, income tax was introduced, prices doubled between 1913 and 1918, and villagers faced forced recruitment into the army.
Crop failures in 1918-19 and 1920-21 and an influenza epidemic added to the suffering; 12 to 13 million people died in the famines and the epidemic.
Mahatma Gandhi returned to India in January 1915. Satyagraha meant fighting injustice through the power of truth and non-violence, appealing to the conscience of the oppressor.

His early satyagrahas: Champaran in Bihar (1917) against the oppressive indigo plantation system, Kheda in Gujarat (1917) for relief from revenue after crop failure and plague, and the Ahmedabad cotton mill workers (1918).

The Rowlatt Act (1919) let the government detain political prisoners without trial for two years. Gandhi called for a nationwide satyagraha with a hartal on 6 April 1919. On 13 April 1919, General Dyer ordered troops to fire on a peaceful crowd gathered at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, and hundreds were killed.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did the Rowlatt Act anger Indians so much?
st: It was hurriedly passed through the Imperial Legislative Council even though all Indian members opposed it.
It allowed people to be detained without trial for up to two years.
That meant the government could jail political workers without proving anything in court.
So Indians saw it as an attack on basic civil rights, and protests spread across the country.
ex.a: It allowed detention without trial and was passed despite united Indian opposition, so it was seen as an attack on basic rights.

topics.rl: Every year on 13 April, people visit the Jallianwala Bagh memorial in Amritsar to remember those who lost their lives there in 1919.

topics.h: Gandhiji's idea was simple: British rule stands because Indians cooperate with it. Stop cooperating, and it will wobble!
p: In Hind Swaraj (1909) Gandhi argued that British rule in India survived only because of Indian cooperation. A Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919, and leaders such as the brothers Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali discussed united action with Gandhi.

At the Calcutta session (September 1920) Gandhi convinced leaders to start non-cooperation in support of Khilafat and swaraj; the programme was adopted at the Nagpur session in December 1920, and the movement began in January 1921.

The plan moved in stages: surrender of government titles, then boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and foreign goods, and full civil disobedience if the government used repression.

In towns, students left government schools, teachers resigned, lawyers gave up their practice and foreign cloth was burnt. The value of imported foreign cloth fell from ₹102 crore to ₹57 crore between 1921 and 1922.

In Awadh, peasants led by Baba Ramchandra protested against talukdars and landlords; the Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up by October 1920. In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh, Alluri Sitarama Raju led a guerrilla struggle. Plantation workers in Assam left the estates, defying the Inland Emigration Act of 1859. Gandhi withdrew the movement in February 1922 after violence at Chauri Chaura.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did the movement in the towns slow down after a while?
st: Khadi cloth was often more expensive than mill cloth, so poor people could not afford it for long.
Boycotting British institutions needed Indian alternatives such as national schools and courts.
These alternatives came up slowly, so students and teachers began going back to government schools and lawyers to courts.
Without affordable substitutes, the boycott was hard to continue.
ex.a: Khadi was costly and Indian alternative institutions were slow to come up, so many people drifted back.

topics.rl: When you see khadi kurtas on sale in a Khadi Gramodyog shop, remember that wearing khadi was once a bold act of protest.

topics.h: Salt! The cheapest thing in your kitchen became the spark that lit a nationwide movement.
p: The Simon Commission arrived in India in 1928 with no Indian member and was greeted with the slogan 'Go back Simon'. In October 1929 Viceroy Lord Irwin offered a vague 'dominion status' and a Round Table Conference.
In December 1929 the Lahore Congress, under Jawaharlal Nehru's presidency, formalised the demand for Purna Swaraj (complete independence), and 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day.

On 31 January 1930 Gandhi sent Lord Irwin a letter with eleven demands, including abolition of the salt tax, with a deadline of 11 March. He then marched with 78 volunteers over 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi in 24 days and broke the salt law on 6 April 1930.

People broke colonial laws: they made salt, picketed liquor shops, boycotted foreign cloth, refused to pay revenue and chaukidari tax, and violated forest laws. Rich peasants like the Patidars of Gujarat and Jats of Uttar Pradesh, businessmen, industrial workers in the Nagpur region, and many women took part.

After the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931, Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in London in December 1931, but talks failed. Dr B.R. Ambedkar organised the Depressed Classes Association in 1930 and sought separate electorates for dalits; the Poona Pact of September 1932 gave them reserved seats, voted for by the general electorate.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did Gandhi choose salt as the symbol of the movement?
st: Salt is used by everyone, rich and poor, in every home.
A tax on salt therefore hurt all Indians, especially the poor.
Making salt from sea water is simple and peaceful, so anyone could break the law non-violently.
So salt united people across classes against a clearly unfair British law.
ex.a: Salt was essential for everyone, so the salt tax was seen as the most oppressive face of British rule, and breaking it united all Indians.

topics.rl: Next time you sprinkle namak on your sabzi, remember that a memorial at Dandi in Gujarat still honours the marchers of 1930.

topics.h: How do millions of people who speak different languages and eat different foods start feeling 'We are one'? Through songs, pictures, stories and flags!
p: Nationalism spreads when people feel they belong to one nation. This feeling grew through shared struggles and through culture: history, fiction, folklore, songs, popular prints and symbols.

The image of India as Bharat Mata was first created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay. In the 1870s he wrote 'Vande Mataram' as a hymn to the motherland; it was later included in his novel Anandamath and was widely sung during the Swadeshi movement in Bengal.

Abanindranath Tagore painted a famous image of Bharat Mata as a calm, composed and spiritual figure. Nationalists also collected folk tales and songs; in Madras, Natesa Sastri published 'The Folklore of Southern India', a four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales.

During the Swadeshi movement in Bengal, a tricolour of red, green and yellow was designed, with eight lotuses for the eight provinces of British India and a crescent moon for Hindus and Muslims. By 1921 Gandhi had designed the Swaraj flag: red, green and white, with a spinning wheel in the centre.

Nationalists reinterpreted history to show India's achievements in art, architecture, science, mathematics, philosophy, crafts and trade in ancient times. They argued that colonial writers had wrongly called Indians backward.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did nationalists put a spinning wheel at the centre of the Swaraj flag?
st: The spinning wheel (charkha) stood for self-help and making our own khadi cloth.
Using khadi meant rejecting foreign, machine-made cloth.
Carrying the flag in marches showed defiance of British rule.
So the charkha turned an everyday tool into a symbol of swadeshi and self-reliance.
ex.a: The spinning wheel symbolised the Gandhian ideal of self-help and swadeshi, so the flag carried that message wherever it went.

topics.rl: The Ashoka Chakra on today's Tiranga replaced the charkha of the Swaraj flag, but the idea of a flag that unites everyone continues.

topics.ch: The Making of a Global World
topics.h: The aloo in your samosa and the mirchi in your chutney are travellers: they came to India from the Americas only after Columbus crossed the Atlantic, a little over five centuries ago!
p: Long before modern times, travellers, traders, priests and pilgrims carried goods, money, skills, ideas and even germs across great distances.

The silk routes, named after the Chinese silk carried along them, linked Asia with Europe and northern Africa. They existed before the Christian era and thrived almost until the 15th century. Chinese pottery and textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia travelled west, while gold and silver flowed east.
Religion and culture also moved along these routes: Buddhism, which emerged in eastern India, spread in several directions through them.

Foods such as potatoes, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes reached Europe and Asia only after Christopher Columbus reached the Americas. In Ireland, poor peasants depended so much on the potato that when disease destroyed the crop in 1845 to 1849, about a million people died of starvation.

By the mid-16th century the Portuguese and Spanish conquest and colonisation of the Americas was well under way. Their most powerful weapon was not guns but germs such as smallpox, to which the local people had no immunity. Silver from mines in Peru and Mexico increased Europe's wealth. Until the 18th century, China and India were among the world's richest countries.

ex.q: Think it through: Why was smallpox more powerful than weapons in the conquest of the Americas?
st: The people of the Americas had been isolated from the rest of the world for a very long time.
So they had no immunity against diseases like smallpox carried by Europeans.
The disease spread quickly and weakened whole communities, ahead of the soldiers themselves.
This made the conquest far easier than fighting alone could have done.
ex.a: Long isolation meant the local people had no immunity to diseases like smallpox, so germs weakened communities before any battle.

topics.rl: Next time you eat aloo paratha or tomato chutney, remember that both potatoes and tomatoes are gifts of the Americas, carried across oceans by trade.

topics.ch: The Making of a Global World
topics.h: In the 1800s the world got 'connected' by three flows: goods, people and money, all moving faster than ever before.
p: Economists describe three flows in the 19th-century world economy: trade (mostly in goods like cloth and wheat), labour (people migrating for work) and capital (investment over long distances).

In Britain the Corn Laws had restricted the import of corn. When they were abolished, cheaper food flowed in from places like Eastern Europe, Russia, America and Australia; British farmers could not compete, and many people moved to cities or overseas. Nearly 50 million people emigrated from Europe to America and Australia in the 19th century.

Technology such as railways, steamships and the telegraph speeded up trade, and refrigerated ships allowed meat to be carried long distances. In India, the British built canal colonies in Punjab to grow wheat and cotton for export.

In 1885 European powers met in Berlin to complete the carving up of Africa. In the late 1880s rinderpest, a cattle disease, spread through Africa and killed 90 per cent of the cattle, destroying livelihoods and forcing Africans into wage labour.

Indentured labourers from eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India and the dry districts of Tamil Nadu went to work in the Caribbean (Trinidad, Guyana, Surinam), Mauritius, Fiji, Ceylon and Malaya. They created new cultures such as Hosay in Trinidad and chutney music. Indentureship was abolished in 1921.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did poor Indians agree to become indentured labourers?
st: Cottage industries were declining and land rents had risen in their home regions.
Many fell into debt and could not survive on their land.
Recruiters promised jobs abroad, sometimes giving false information about the work and living conditions.
So hardship at home pushed people to accept contracts to work in faraway plantations, mines and construction sites.
ex.a: Poverty, debt and declining home industries pushed them, while recruiters' promises pulled them to distant lands.

topics.rl: Many people of Indian origin in Fiji, Mauritius, Trinidad and Guyana are descendants of indentured labourers, and some still celebrate Diwali and sing Bhojpuri songs there.

topics.ch: The Making of a Global World
topics.t: The inter-war economy and the Great Depression
topics.h: One terrible war, one car factory in Detroit and one big economic crash: the years 1914 to the 1930s changed the world economy.
p: The First World War (1914 to 1918) was fought between the Allies (Britain, France and Russia, later joined by the US) and the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey). It was the first modern industrial war, using machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons.

Britain borrowed large sums from US banks and the US public, so the US turned from an international debtor into an international creditor. After the war, Britain faced huge debts and unemployment, and lost much of its Indian cotton market to Japan.

In the US, Henry Ford adapted the assembly line to car-making in Detroit and produced the T-Model Ford. In January 1914 he raised the daily wage of his workers to $5, roughly double the earlier wage. Mass production lowered costs, and hire purchase let people buy on credit.

The Great Depression began around 1929 and lasted till the mid-1930s. Agricultural overproduction made prices fall, and when the US cut back its overseas loans, many countries faced crisis. In the US, between 1929 and 1932 about 110,000 companies collapsed.

In India, between 1928 and 1934 exports and imports nearly halved and wheat prices fell by 50 per cent. Peasants could not pay revenue and fell into debt, and India exported precious metals, notably gold.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did Indian peasants suffer badly in the Great Depression even though prices fell?
st: Peasants sold crops in the market, so falling prices cut their incomes sharply.
But the colonial government did not reduce revenue demands.
So peasants had to pay the same tax out of much smaller earnings.
Many used up savings, mortgaged land or sold gold and silver jewellery to survive.
ex.a: Their crop prices and incomes fell, but revenue demands did not, so they fell into debt and sold land and jewellery.

topics.rl: When people buy a phone or a scooter on EMIs today, they are using credit, much like the hire purchase that spread in 1920s America.

topics.ch: The Making of a Global World
topics.h: After the Second World War, world leaders met at a hotel in the small town of Bretton Woods, USA, to design new rules for money. Their plan shaped decades of growth.
p: The Second World War (1939 to 1945) was fought between the Axis powers (mainly Germany, Japan and Italy) and the Allies (Britain, France, the Soviet Union and the US). After it, the US emerged as the dominant economic, political and military power.

Economists drew two lessons from the inter-war years: mass production can last only with mass consumption, which needs high and steady incomes and employment; and a country's economic links with the outside world must be managed carefully.

In July 1944 the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference was held at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire, USA. It set up the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to deal with members' external surpluses and deficits, and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank) to finance post-war reconstruction.

The IMF and World Bank, called the Bretton Woods twins, began financial operations in 1947. Under the Bretton Woods system, exchange rates were fixed and the US dollar was anchored to gold at $35 per ounce. The US had an effective veto over key decisions.

Many newly independent developing countries, still facing poverty, joined together as the Group of 77 (G-77) to demand a New International Economic Order (NIEO), seeking real control over their natural resources, fairer prices for raw materials and better access to markets.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did newly independent countries form the G-77?
st: Many former colonies had been held back by long periods of colonial rule.
The IMF and World Bank were dominated by the rich Western countries.
Developing countries felt the system did not serve their needs.
So they joined together to demand a fairer New International Economic Order.
ex.a: They wanted a fairer world economic system, so they organised as the G-77 and demanded an NIEO.

topics.rl: India is a member of the IMF and the World Bank, and news reports about World Bank loans for Indian projects like roads or clean water continue this post-war story.

topics.h: Before big factories with chimneys, cloth for the world market was spun and woven in village cottages, with merchants running from hut to hut!
p: Proto-industrialisation was the phase before factories, when there was large-scale production for an international market that was not based in factories. It is seen in England and Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries.

Merchants moved to the countryside because in towns powerful crafts and trade guilds controlled production, regulated prices and competition, and kept new people out. Peasants and artisans in villages, short of land and income, welcomed merchants' advances to produce goods.

A merchant clothier bought wool from a wool stapler and took it to spinners; the yarn then went to weavers, fullers and dyers, and the cloth was finished in London before export. Merchants, not the workers, controlled the whole chain.

Factories grew in England from the late 18th century. Imports of raw cotton rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds by 1787. Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill, and James Watt improved Newcomen's steam engine and patented his new engine in 1781; Matthew Boulton manufactured it.

Change was slow. In Victorian Britain labour was cheap and plentiful, so many industrialists preferred hand labour, especially in seasonal industries. The upper classes valued handmade goods as a sign of refinement. When James Hargreaves' spinning jenny (1764) came in, women who survived on hand spinning attacked the new machines.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did many Victorian industrialists prefer workers to machines?
st: Machines were costly to buy and repair, and they often broke down.
There was no shortage of poor workers willing to work for low wages.
Many industries were seasonal, so employers wanted workers only for part of the year.
Hand labour also gave the variety and fine finish that rich buyers wanted.
ex.a: Labour was cheap and plentiful, machines were costly and inflexible, and many buyers wanted handmade goods.

topics.rl: Today, handloom saris from Banaras, Kanchipuram or Pochampally are still prized because they are handmade, just as rich Victorians valued handmade goods.

topics.h: Indian cotton and silk once dressed the world. Then came Manchester's machine cloth, and later India's own mills fought back.
p: Before machine industries, Indian silk and cotton dominated the international textile market. Ports like Surat on the Gujarat coast, Masulipatam on the Coromandel coast and Hoogly in Bengal linked India with the world. As the East India Company gained power, new ports at Bombay and Calcutta grew.

The Company appointed paid servants called gomasthas to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine the quality of cloth. Weavers who took advances could not sell to other buyers, and clashes broke out in many villages in Carnatic and Bengal.

In the 19th century, British cotton goods flooded India. Indian weavers lost export markets, their local market shrank, and raw cotton became costly when the American Civil War (1860s) made Britain buy more Indian cotton.

The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in 1854; the first jute mill in Bengal in 1855; the first spinning and weaving mill of Madras began production in 1874. Early entrepreneurs included Dwarkanath Tagore in Bengal and Parsis like Dinshaw Petit and Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee Tata in Bombay. The Tata Iron and Steel works began production at Jamshedpur in 1912, and Seth Hukumchand set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in 1917.

Mills hired workers through jobbers, often trusted old workers who brought people from their villages but later demanded gifts and controlled their lives. Industry grew with the Swadeshi movement's boycott of foreign cloth and during the First World War, when Manchester imports fell and Indian mills supplied army needs. Handloom production also survived and grew, helped by the fly shuttle.

ex.q: Think it through: How did the First World War help Indian factories grow?
st: British mills were busy producing for war needs, so exports of Manchester cloth to India fell.
Indian mills suddenly had a large home market to supply.
They also got orders for army needs: jute bags, cloth for uniforms, tents, leather boots and saddles.
Production grew so much that Manchester never fully regained its old position in India.
ex.a: Manchester imports fell and Indian mills supplied war needs, so they expanded and gained the home market.

topics.rl: Jamshedpur in Jharkhand, named after Jamsetji Tata, grew into a big industrial city around the steel works that began production in 1912.

topics.h: Making cloth is one thing; making people want to buy it is another. Welcome to the world of labels, calendars and advertisements!
p: New producers had to win buyers. Advertisements make products seem desirable and necessary, and try to shape people's minds and create new needs.
Manchester industrialists put labels on cloth bundles. Words like 'MADE IN MANCHESTER' in bold letters were meant to make buyers trust the quality.

Labels also carried images and beautiful pictures. Indian gods and goddesses, such as Krishna or Saraswati, appeared on labels so the product seemed to have divine approval and felt familiar to Indian buyers.

Manufacturers printed calendars to popularise their products. Unlike newspapers, calendars were used even by people who could not read, and they hung all year in tea shops, homes and offices. Images of historical figures such as emperors and nawabs were also used to give products a sense of respect and tradition.
When Indian manufacturers advertised, the nationalist message was clear: if you care for the nation, buy products that Indians produce. Advertisements became a vehicle for the swadeshi idea.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did manufacturers choose calendars rather than only newspaper ads?
st: Many people in India at that time could not read newspapers.
A calendar is useful, so people kept it on the wall for the whole year.
It was seen daily in tea shops, homes and offices.
So the product's picture and name reached people every day, even those who could not read.
ex.a: Calendars were used all year and seen daily, even by people who could not read, so the brand stayed in front of them.

topics.rl: Look around a kirana shop or a dhaba today: free calendars with company logos and festival images are still a popular way to advertise.

topics.ch: Print Culture and the Modern World
topics.t: The first printed books: East Asia and Europe
topics.h: Before printing, every single book was copied by hand. One Bible could take months! Then woodblocks and a clever German goldsmith changed everything.
p: The earliest print technology came from China, Japan and Korea. From about AD 594, books in China were printed by rubbing paper against the inked surface of woodblocks. Since only one side of the thin paper could be printed, it was folded and stitched into an 'accordion book'. For a long time the imperial state was the biggest producer of printed material, such as textbooks for the civil service examination.

Buddhist missionaries from China brought hand printing to Japan around AD 768-770. The oldest Japanese book, printed in AD 868, is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, with six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations.

Marco Polo returned to Italy from China in 1295 with knowledge of woodblock printing. Paper reached Europe through the silk route. Earlier, luxury editions were handwritten on vellum, a parchment made from animal skin.

Johann Gutenberg, who grew up seeing wine and olive presses and later learnt to polish stones and make lead moulds, perfected his printing system by 1448. The first book he printed was the Bible: about 180 copies, which took three years to produce.
Between 1450 and 1550, printing presses were set up in most countries of Europe. This 'print revolution' made books cheaper and created a new reading public in place of a mainly 'hearing public'.

ex.q: Think it through: How did the printing press change who could read books?
st: Hand-copying was slow and costly, so books were few and expensive.
The press could print many copies quickly, so the time and cost of each book fell sharply.
Cheaper books reached markets and many more people could buy them.
So reading spread beyond the elite, and a new reading public was born.
ex.a: It made books faster and cheaper to produce, so many more ordinary people could buy and read them.

topics.rl: When your school prints hundreds of copies of a question paper in a few minutes, it is using the great-great-grandchildren of Gutenberg's press.

topics.ch: Print Culture and the Modern World
topics.h: India already had beautiful handwritten manuscripts on palm leaves. Then a ship to Goa brought a strange new machine: the printing press.
p: India had a rich tradition of handwritten manuscripts in Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian and many vernacular languages, written on palm leaves or handmade paper. They were costly and fragile, so they were not widely used in everyday life.

The printing press first came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid-16th century. Jesuit priests learnt Konkani, and by 1674 about 50 books had been printed in the Konkani and Kannada languages.

Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin, and in 1713 the first Malayalam book. By 1710, Dutch Protestant missionaries had printed 32 Tamil texts, many of them translations of older works.

In 1780 James Augustus Hickey began editing the Bengal Gazette, a weekly magazine. He published advertisements and also gossip about the Company's senior officials. Governor-General Warren Hastings persecuted him and encouraged officially approved newspapers.
The first Indian newspaper to appear was the weekly Bengal Gazette brought out by Gangadhar Bhattacharya, who was close to Rammohun Roy.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did Warren Hastings act against Hickey?
st: Hickey's paper published gossip about the Company's senior officials in India.
Such reports could damage the image of the colonial government.
Hastings wanted to control what was printed about British rule.
So he persecuted Hickey and encouraged newspapers that would protect the government's image.
ex.a: Hickey's paper criticised and gossiped about Company officials, so Hastings tried to silence him and backed approved papers instead.

topics.rl: Many Indian newspapers today are more than a hundred years old. Their story began in the bustling presses of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.

topics.ch: Print Culture and the Modern World
topics.t: Print, reform and revolution in Europe
topics.h: One monk's list of 95 complaints, printed thousands of times, helped split the Church in Europe. Print had become powerful!
p: Not everyone welcomed print. The Latin scholar and Catholic reformer Erasmus worried that books would spread rebellious and irreligious ideas.

In 1517 the religious reformer Martin Luther wrote the Ninety Five Theses criticising many practices of the Roman Catholic Church. Printed copies spread widely, leading to division in the Church and the beginning of the Protestant Reformation. Luther said, 'Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one.'
Worried by the spread of new ideas, the Roman Church began keeping an Index of Prohibited Books from 1558.

By the 17th and 18th centuries literacy grew in Europe. Pedlars sold cheap chapbooks in England, and the Bibliotheque Bleue in France offered low-priced small books. Almanacs, ballads, newspapers and periodicals spread too. The writer Louise-Sebastien Mercier called the printing press 'the most powerful engine of progress'.

Many historians argue that print helped bring about the French Revolution: it popularised the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers like Voltaire and Rousseau, created a culture of dialogue and debate, and spread literature that mocked royalty. In the 19th century Richard M. Hoe of New York perfected the power-driven cylindrical press, which could print 8,000 sheets per hour.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did print help the ideas of the Reformation spread so fast?
st: Before print, a reformer's ideas spread slowly by hand-copied letters and sermons.
Luther's Ninety Five Theses were printed in large numbers and read widely.
People could read and discuss the ideas themselves in many places at once.
So the debate spread quickly, leading to the Protestant Reformation.
ex.a: Print reproduced Luther's writings in large numbers, so many people read and debated them at the same time.

topics.rl: Today, a post or a video can spread around India in hours. In the 16th century, the printing press did something similar for Luther's ideas.

topics.ch: Print Culture and the Modern World
topics.h: In 19th-century India, presses became busy debate halls on paper, where reformers, women writers and workers all found a voice.
p: From the early 19th century, print carried lively debates on religion and society. Rammohun Roy published the Sambad Kaumudi from 1821, while Hindu orthodox groups commissioned the Samachar Chandrika. In 1822 two Persian newspapers, Jam-i-Jahan Nama and Shamsul Akhbar, appeared, and in the same year the Gujarati newspaper Bombay Samachar was published.

The Deoband Seminary, founded in 1867, published thousands of fatwas guiding Muslims in daily life. The first printed edition of Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas came out from Calcutta in 1810. Presses like the Naval Kishore Press at Lucknow and the Shri Venkateshwar Press in Bombay published religious texts in vernacular languages, so people could read them easily.

Women became readers and writers. Rashsundari Debi learnt to read secretly in her kitchen and wrote Amar Jiban, published in 1876, the first full-length autobiography in the Bengali language. In the 1880s Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai in Maharashtra wrote about the hard lives of upper-caste Hindu women, especially widows.

Reformers wrote against caste injustice: Jyotiba Phule wrote Gulamgiri (1871); B.R. Ambedkar in Maharashtra and E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar) in Madras also wrote powerfully on caste. Kashibaba, a Kanpur mill worker, wrote and published Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal in 1938.

The colonial state tried to control print. After 1857, the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, modelled on the Irish Press Laws, gave the government wide powers to censor the vernacular press. When Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote with sympathy in his paper Kesari about Punjab revolutionaries deported in 1907, he was imprisoned in 1908, sparking widespread protests.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did the British pass the Vernacular Press Act in 1878?
st: After 1857, the colonial government became suspicious of the Indian press.
Vernacular newspapers were becoming more numerous and assertively nationalist.
They criticised colonial policies in languages ordinary Indians could read.
So the Act gave the government power to censor reports and editorials and punish critical papers.
ex.a: Vernacular papers were spreading criticism of colonial rule to ordinary readers, so the government took powers to censor them.

topics.rl: A free press that reports and debates public issues is part of Indian democracy today, protected by the freedom of speech and expression in our Constitution.

qa.q: In which year did the French Revolution begin?
qa.e: The French Revolution began in 1789. 1815 is the Treaty of Vienna and 1848 is the year of the liberal revolutions.

qa.q: What did the French Revolutionaries mean by 'la patrie'?
qa.a: The fatherland
qa.e: La patrie means the fatherland; le citoyen means the citizen. Both ideas stressed a united community with equal rights.

qa.q: The French Revolution transferred sovereignty from whom to whom?
qa.a: From the monarch to the body of French citizens
qa.e: Before 1789 the king held supreme power. The Revolution declared that the people, as citizens, formed the nation and held sovereignty.

qa.q: Which language was promoted as the common language of the French nation?
qa.a: French as spoken and written in Paris
qa.e: Regional dialects were discouraged and Parisian French became the common language, helping unify the nation.

qa.q: In which year was Napoleon's Civil Code, also called the Napoleonic Code, introduced?
qa.e: The Civil Code was introduced in 1804, after Napoleon came to power.

qa.q: Which of these did the Civil Code of 1804 do?
qa.a: Made everyone equal before the law and secured the right to property
qa.e: The Code abolished privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property.

qa.q: Why did many people in areas conquered by Napoleon turn against French rule?
qa.a: Increased taxation, censorship and forced conscription into French armies
qa.e: The useful reforms were outweighed in people's minds by heavy taxes, censorship and being forced to fight in French armies.

qa.q: Which statement best describes a nation-state?
qa.a: Most of its citizens share a sense of common identity and history
qa.e: In a nation-state, citizens see themselves as one community. A dynastic empire, by contrast, holds many peoples together under one ruling family.

qa.q: The word 'liberalism' comes from the Latin root 'liber'. What does 'liber' mean?
qa.a: Free
qa.e: Liber means free, which is why liberalism stood for individual freedom.

qa.q: What was the Zollverein of 1834?
qa.a: A customs union formed at the initiative of Prussia
qa.e: The Zollverein was a customs union joined by most German states. It removed tariff barriers between them.

qa.q: The Zollverein reduced the number of currencies in the German states from over thirty to how many?
qa.e: It brought the currencies down from over thirty to just two, making trade far easier.

qa.q: Who hosted the Congress of Vienna in 1815?
qa.a: Duke Metternich, the Austrian Chancellor
qa.e: Metternich hosted the Congress, which aimed to undo the changes brought by Napoleon.

qa.q: Which dynasty did the Treaty of Vienna restore to power in France?
qa.a: The Bourbon dynasty
qa.e: The Bourbons, who had been removed during the French Revolution, were brought back in 1815.

qa.q: Giuseppe Mazzini founded the secret society Young Italy in which city?
qa.a: Marseilles
qa.e: Young Italy was founded in Marseilles. His other society, Young Europe, was founded in Berne.

qa.q: Who described Mazzini as 'the most dangerous enemy of our social order'?
qa.a: Duke Metternich
qa.e: Metternich, the leading conservative of the age, saw Mazzini's revolutionary ideas as a threat to the old order.

qa.q: In revolutionary France, who were given the right to vote and to be elected?
qa.a: Only property-owning men
qa.e: Liberal ideas of equality did not yet mean universal suffrage: voting was limited to men who owned property.

qa.q: Which treaty recognised Greece as an independent nation in 1832?
qa.a: The Treaty of Constantinople
qa.e: The Greek war of independence began in 1821 and the Treaty of Constantinople of 1832 recognised Greece as independent.

qa.q: After the July Revolution of 1830 in France, who headed the new constitutional monarchy?
qa.a: Louis Philippe
qa.e: Liberal revolutionaries overthrew the Bourbon kings and installed a constitutional monarchy with Louis Philippe at its head.

qa.q: How many elected representatives took their places in the Frankfurt Parliament on 18 May 1848?
qa.e: 831 elected representatives marched to the Church of St Paul in Frankfurt.

qa.q: To whom did the Frankfurt Parliament offer the crown of a united Germany?
qa.a: Friedrich Wilhelm IV, King of Prussia
qa.e: The crown was offered to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, who rejected it. William I later became German Emperor in 1871.

qa.q: According to Johann Gottfried Herder, where was true German culture to be found?
qa.a: Among the common people (das volk)
qa.e: Herder believed folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances of ordinary people expressed the true spirit of the nation.

qa.q: Why did speaking Polish become a symbol of struggle in the 19th century?
qa.a: Poland was under Russian rule and Russian was imposed, so using Polish showed resistance
qa.e: Under Russian rule, Polish was forced out of schools and Russian was imposed everywhere, and an armed rebellion in 1831 was crushed. Using Polish for church gatherings and religious teaching became a symbol of the struggle against Russian dominance.

qa.q: When the Republic was proclaimed in France in 1848, the vote was given to all adult males above what age?
qa.e: The National Assembly granted suffrage to all adult males above 21 and guaranteed the right to work.

qa.q: What role were women allowed at the Frankfurt Parliament?
qa.a: Only observers in the visitors' gallery
qa.e: Though many women had taken part in the liberal movement, they were denied the right to vote and sat only in the visitors' gallery.

qa.q: Who was the chief minister of Prussia who led the unification of Germany?
qa.a: Otto von Bismarck
qa.e: Bismarck, with the Prussian army and bureaucracy, was the architect of German unification.

qa.q: Who was proclaimed German Emperor in January 1871?
qa.a: William I, King of Prussia
qa.e: The Prussian king William I became German Emperor. Bismarck was his chief minister, not the emperor.

qa.q: Where was the new German Empire proclaimed in 1871?
qa.a: In the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles
qa.e: The ceremony took place at the Palace of Versailles in France, after Prussia's victory over France.

qa.q: Prussia fought three wars over seven years to unify Germany. Against which countries?
qa.a: Austria, Denmark and France
qa.e: Prussia defeated Austria, Denmark and France, and these victories completed unification.

qa.q: Before unification, which was the only Italian state ruled by an Italian princely house?
qa.a: Sardinia-Piedmont
qa.e: The north was under Austria, the centre under the Pope and the south under the Bourbon kings of Spain; only Sardinia-Piedmont had an Italian ruling house.

qa.q: How did Cavour help bring about Italian unification?
qa.a: He made a diplomatic alliance with France that helped defeat Austria in 1859
qa.e: Cavour was neither a revolutionary nor a democrat; he used diplomacy. Garibaldi led the volunteers, Mazzini founded Young Italy and Victor Emmanuel II became king.

qa.q: In 1860, Garibaldi's armed volunteers marched into which region?
qa.a: South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies
qa.e: Garibaldi won the support of local peasants and drove out the Spanish Bourbon rulers from the south.

qa.q: In which year was Victor Emmanuel II proclaimed king of united Italy?
qa.e: 1859 was the defeat of Austria, 1860 Garibaldi's march, and 1861 the proclamation of Victor Emmanuel II as king.

qa.q: When did Mahatma Gandhi return to India from South Africa?
qa.a: January 1915
qa.e: Gandhi came back in January 1915 and soon began local satyagrahas.

qa.q: What is the main idea of satyagraha?
qa.a: Fighting injustice through the power of truth and non-violence
qa.e: Satyagraha stresses the power of truth. The satyagrahi wins the battle through non-violence by appealing to the conscience of the oppressor.

qa.q: Gandhi's 1917 satyagraha in Champaran, Bihar, was against what?
qa.a: The oppressive indigo plantation system
qa.e: In Champaran he inspired peasants against the oppressive plantation system. The Ahmedabad satyagraha (1918) was for mill workers.

qa.q: Why did peasants of Kheda district in Gujarat need help in 1917?
qa.a: Crop failure and a plague epidemic left them unable to pay land revenue
qa.e: Gandhi organised satyagraha to support Kheda peasants who demanded relaxation of revenue collection.

qa.q: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed the government to detain political prisoners without trial for how many years?
qa.e: The Act allowed detention without trial for two years, which Indians saw as deeply unjust.

qa.q: On which date did Gandhi call for a nationwide hartal against the Rowlatt Act?
qa.a: 6 April 1919
qa.e: The hartal was on 6 April 1919. 13 April 1919 is Jallianwala Bagh, and 6 April 1930 is when Gandhi made salt at Dandi.

qa.q: Where did the Jallianwala Bagh incident take place?
qa.a: Amritsar
qa.e: Jallianwala Bagh is in Amritsar, Punjab. On 13 April 1919 troops under General Dyer fired on the gathered crowd.

qa.q: Which of these was a hardship caused in India by the First World War?
qa.a: Prices doubled between 1913 and 1918
qa.e: War spending raised taxes and duties, introduced income tax and pushed prices up, while villages faced forced recruitment.

qa.q: In which book did Gandhi argue that British rule survived only because of Indian cooperation?
qa.a: Hind Swaraj
qa.e: Gandhi wrote Hind Swaraj in 1909. Anandamath is by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, Gulamgiri by Jyotiba Phule and Amar Jiban by Rashsundari Debi.

qa.q: At which Congress session was the Non-Cooperation programme adopted?
qa.a: Nagpur, December 1920
qa.e: Gandhi convinced leaders at Calcutta in September 1920, and the programme was finally adopted at Nagpur in December 1920.

qa.q: Which was one of the planned stages of the Non-Cooperation Movement?
qa.a: Surrender of titles awarded by the government
qa.e: The movement began with surrendering titles and moved to boycotts. Salt-making belonged to the Civil Disobedience Movement, and violence was against Gandhi's method.

qa.q: Between 1921 and 1922, the value of imported foreign cloth fell from ₹102 crore to how many crore rupees?
qa.e: The boycott nearly halved foreign cloth imports, from ₹102 crore to ₹57 crore.

qa.q: Who led the peasant movement in Awadh against talukdars and landlords?
qa.a: Baba Ramchandra
qa.e: Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi who had earlier been an indentured labourer in Fiji, led the Awadh peasants. Alluri Sitarama Raju led the Gudem Hills struggle.

qa.q: Alluri Sitarama Raju led a guerrilla movement in which region?
qa.a: The Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh
qa.e: In the early 1920s Raju led tribal people of the Gudem Hills against restrictions on their forests.

qa.q: Why did Gandhi call off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922?
qa.a: It was turning violent, as seen at Chauri Chaura
qa.e: After a clash at Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur turned violent, Gandhi felt satyagrahis needed proper training before mass struggles.

qa.q: Which leaders formed the Swaraj Party to return to council politics after the movement?
qa.a: C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru
qa.e: C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party. Younger leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pressed for radical mass agitation and full independence.

qa.q: Why was the Simon Commission opposed in India?
qa.a: It did not have a single Indian member
qa.e: The Commission was to look into India's constitutional system, yet no Indian was on it, so it was met with 'Go back Simon'.

qa.q: Which Congress session formalised the demand for Purna Swaraj?
qa.a: Lahore, December 1929, under Jawaharlal Nehru
qa.e: Jawaharlal Nehru presided over the Lahore session of December 1929, which demanded complete independence.

qa.q: Which day was celebrated as Independence Day after the Lahore session?
qa.a: 26 January 1930
qa.e: 26 January 1930 was declared Independence Day; that is why our Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950.

qa.q: How many volunteers marched with Gandhi from Sabarmati to Dandi?
qa.e: There were 78 volunteers. The march covered over 240 miles in 24 days, and Gandhi's letter had 11 demands.

qa.q: On which date did Gandhi break the salt law at Dandi?
qa.a: 6 April 1930
qa.e: He reached Dandi and made salt by boiling sea water on 6 April 1930. 31 January was the letter, 11 March the deadline.

qa.q: How was the Civil Disobedience Movement different from the Non-Cooperation Movement?
qa.a: People were asked not only to refuse cooperation but also to break colonial laws
qa.e: Non-Cooperation meant withdrawing cooperation; Civil Disobedience went further by deliberately breaking laws such as the salt law.

qa.q: Which business organisation was set up by Indian industrialists in 1927?
qa.a: Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries (FICCI)
qa.e: Industrialists like Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G.D. Birla formed FICCI in 1927 to protect Indian business interests.

qa.q: What did the Poona Pact of September 1932 give the Depressed Classes?
qa.a: Reserved seats in legislative councils, voted for by the general electorate
qa.e: Ambedkar had demanded separate electorates; Gandhi opposed this. The Poona Pact settled on reserved seats elected by the general electorate.

qa.q: Who first created the image of Bharat Mata as an identity of India?
qa.a: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
qa.e: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay created the image and wrote 'Vande Mataram' in the 1870s.

qa.q: 'Vande Mataram' was later included in which novel?
qa.a: Anandamath
qa.e: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay included the hymn in his novel Anandamath. It was widely sung in the Swadeshi movement in Bengal.

qa.q: How did Abanindranath Tagore portray Bharat Mata in his painting?
qa.a: As a calm, composed, spiritual figure
qa.e: His Bharat Mata is an ascetic figure who is calm and divine, giving food, clothing, learning and spiritual wisdom.

qa.q: What did Natesa Sastri publish?
qa.a: A four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales
qa.e: His 'The Folklore of Southern India' saw folklore as national literature reflecting people's real thoughts.

qa.q: On the Swadeshi movement flag of Bengal, what did the eight lotuses stand for?
qa.a: The eight provinces of British India
qa.e: The eight lotuses stood for the eight provinces, and the crescent moon represented Hindus and Muslims.

qa.q: What was at the centre of the Swaraj flag designed by Gandhi by 1921?
qa.a: A spinning wheel
qa.e: The Swaraj flag had a spinning wheel, symbolising self-help. The Ashoka Chakra is on today's national flag.

qa.q: What were the colours of Gandhi's Swaraj flag of 1921?
qa.a: Red, green and white
qa.e: The Swaraj flag was red, green and white. Red, green and yellow was the Swadeshi flag of Bengal; saffron, white and green is today's Tiranga.

qa.q: Why did Indian nationalists write about India's achievements in ancient times?
qa.a: To counter the colonial view that Indians were backward and to build pride
qa.e: By recalling achievements in art, science, mathematics, philosophy and trade, they encouraged people to take pride in the past and struggle against British rule.

qa.q: Why are the silk routes called by that name?
qa.a: Chinese silk was one of the main goods carried along them
qa.e: Historians named them after the valuable Chinese silk cargoes, though many other goods also travelled on them.

qa.q: The silk routes linked Asia with which regions?
qa.a: Europe and northern Africa
qa.e: These land and sea routes joined vast regions of Asia with Europe and northern Africa.

qa.q: Which religion, born in eastern India, spread in several directions along the silk routes?
qa.a: Buddhism
qa.e: Buddhism emerged in eastern India and spread through the silk routes. Christian missionaries and Muslim preachers also later travelled these routes.

qa.q: Which of these foods reached India only after Columbus reached the Americas?
qa.a: Chillies
qa.e: Chillies, potatoes, tomatoes, maize and groundnuts came from the Americas. Black pepper, rice and sugarcane were grown in Asia much earlier.

qa.q: Why did about a million people die in Ireland between 1845 and 1849?
qa.a: A disease destroyed the potato crop on which poor peasants depended
qa.e: Poor Irish peasants depended heavily on potatoes, so when disease destroyed the crop, famine followed.

qa.q: What was the most powerful 'weapon' of the Spanish conquerors in the Americas?
qa.a: Germs such as smallpox
qa.e: Isolated for long, the local people had no immunity against smallpox, which spread deep into the continent.

qa.q: From where did silver flow to Europe after the conquest of the Americas?
qa.a: Mines in Peru and Mexico
qa.e: Silver from Peru and Mexico greatly added to Europe's wealth and financed its trade with Asia.

qa.q: Which countries were among the richest in the world until the 18th century?
qa.a: China and India
qa.e: China and India were pre-eminent in Asian trade until the 18th century.

qa.q: Which three flows did economists identify in the 19th-century world economy?
qa.a: Trade, labour and capital
qa.e: Trade in goods, migration of labour and movement of capital for investment were the three flows that knitted economies together.

qa.q: What happened after the Corn Laws were abolished in Britain?
qa.a: Cheaper food was imported and British agriculture could not compete
qa.e: Food could now be imported more cheaply than it was grown in Britain, so large areas went uncultivated and people left for cities or overseas.

qa.q: About how many people emigrated from Europe to America and Australia in the 19th century?
qa.a: Nearly 50 million
qa.e: Nearly 50 million Europeans left for America and Australia, looking for land and work.

qa.q: Why did the British build canal colonies in Punjab?
qa.a: To turn semi-desert land into fertile land for growing wheat and cotton for export
qa.e: Canals irrigated semi-desert wastes so that Punjab could grow export crops like wheat and cotton.

qa.q: What was the main purpose of the Berlin conference of 1885?
qa.a: European powers met to complete the carving up of Africa
qa.e: At Berlin in 1885 the big European powers divided African territory among themselves.

qa.q: What was rinderpest?
qa.a: A fast-spreading cattle disease that killed most of Africa's cattle
qa.e: Rinderpest arrived in Africa in the late 1880s and killed 90 per cent of the cattle, destroying African livelihoods.

qa.q: Who was an indentured labourer?
qa.a: A bonded labourer under contract to work for an employer for a fixed period
qa.e: Indentured labourers signed contracts to work for a specific time, often to pay for their passage, and could not leave freely.

qa.q: In which year was indentured labour from India abolished?
qa.e: Indian nationalist leaders opposed it as a new system of slavery, and it was abolished in 1921.

qa.q: Which countries formed the Central Powers in the First World War?
qa.a: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey
qa.e: The Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey. Germany, Italy and Japan were the Axis powers of the Second World War.

qa.q: Why is the First World War called the first modern industrial war?
qa.a: It used machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons made by modern industry
qa.e: Modern industry supplied weapons on a huge scale, and the war mobilised millions of soldiers.

qa.q: How did the First World War change the US's economic position?
qa.a: The US became an international creditor
qa.e: Britain and others borrowed from US banks and the public, so after the war the US was owed more by others than it owed.

qa.q: In 1914, Henry Ford raised his workers' daily wage to how many US dollars?
qa.e: Ford raised the daily wage to $5, roughly doubling it, to keep workers on the fast, tiring assembly line. $35 is the price of gold per ounce under Bretton Woods.

qa.q: Roughly when did the Great Depression take place?
qa.a: Around 1929 to the mid-1930s
qa.e: The Depression began around 1929 and lasted until the mid-1930s. 1914 to 1918 was the First World War.

qa.q: Which was a cause of the Great Depression?
qa.a: Agricultural overproduction that made farm prices fall
qa.e: Too much farm produce pushed prices down, and the fall in US overseas loans spread the crisis to many countries.

qa.q: Between 1928 and 1934, by what percentage did wheat prices fall in India?
qa.e: Wheat prices fell by half, cutting peasants' incomes while revenue demands stayed the same.

qa.q: Which precious metal did India export in large amounts during the Depression?
qa.a: Gold
qa.e: Distressed peasants sold gold jewellery, and India exported precious metals, notably gold.

qa.q: Which countries were the main Axis powers in the Second World War?
qa.a: Germany, Japan and Italy
qa.e: The Axis powers were mainly Germany, Japan and Italy. Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey were the Central Powers of the First World War.

qa.q: Where was the conference that set up the IMF and the World Bank held?
qa.a: Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, USA
qa.e: The United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference met at Bretton Woods in July 1944.

qa.q: In which year was the Bretton Woods conference held?
qa.e: It met in July 1944. The IMF and World Bank began operations in 1947.

qa.q: What was the main purpose of the International Monetary Fund?
qa.a: To deal with the external surpluses and deficits of member nations
qa.e: The IMF dealt with balance of payments problems; financing reconstruction was the World Bank's job.

qa.q: Which institution was set up to finance post-war reconstruction?
qa.a: The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank)
qa.e: The IBRD, popularly called the World Bank, financed rebuilding after the war.

qa.q: Under the Bretton Woods system, the US dollar was fixed to gold at how many US dollars per ounce?
qa.e: The dollar was anchored to gold at $35 per ounce, and other currencies were fixed to the dollar.

qa.q: Which lesson did economists learn from the inter-war experience?
qa.a: Mass production can be sustained only with mass consumption, needing high and steady incomes
qa.e: The Depression showed that if people lack steady incomes, they cannot buy what factories produce.

qa.q: What did the G-77 demand?
qa.a: A New International Economic Order
qa.e: The G-77 sought an NIEO giving developing countries real control over their resources and fairer terms of trade.

qa.q: What does 'proto-industrialisation' refer to?
qa.a: Large-scale production for an international market before the factory age
qa.e: Proto means early or first. It was large-scale production for international markets, done in homes and workshops, not factories.

qa.q: Why did merchants in 17th and 18th century Europe find it hard to expand production in towns?
qa.a: Powerful crafts and trade guilds controlled production and kept new people out
qa.e: Guilds trained craftspeople, regulated prices and competition and restricted entry, often with monopoly rights from rulers.

qa.q: Who controlled the whole cloth-making chain in proto-industrial England?
qa.a: The merchant clothier
qa.e: The merchant clothier bought wool, paid spinners, weavers, fullers and dyers, and sold the finished cloth, so he controlled production.

qa.q: Imports of raw cotton into Britain rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to how many million pounds by 1787?
qa.e: Raw cotton imports soared to 22 million pounds, showing how fast the cotton industry was growing.

qa.q: Who created the cotton mill?
qa.a: Richard Arkwright
qa.e: Arkwright's mill brought all processes under one roof and management. Watt improved the steam engine; Ford built cars much later.

qa.q: In which year did James Watt patent his improved steam engine?
qa.e: Watt patented it in 1781. 1764 is the spinning jenny, and 1854 is Bombay's first cotton mill.

qa.q: Why did women in the woollen industry attack the spinning jenny?
qa.a: They survived on hand spinning and feared losing their jobs
qa.e: The jenny let one worker turn many spindles at once, which threatened the livelihood of hand spinners.

qa.q: Why did upper classes in Victorian Britain prefer handmade goods?
qa.a: They saw them as a symbol of refinement and class
qa.e: Handmade products were finely finished and individually designed, so the rich valued them; machine-made goods went largely to the colonies.

qa.q: Who were gomasthas?
qa.a: Paid servants of the East India Company who supervised weavers and checked cloth quality
qa.e: Gomasthas supervised weavers, collected supplies and examined quality, and often treated weavers harshly.

qa.q: Which pre-colonial port was on the Coromandel coast?
qa.a: Masulipatam
qa.e: Masulipatam was on the Coromandel coast, Surat on the Gujarat coast and Hoogly in Bengal. Bombay grew later under the Company.

qa.q: Why did raw cotton become costly for Indian weavers in the 1860s?
qa.a: The American Civil War cut cotton supplies from the US, so Britain bought more Indian cotton
qa.e: With US cotton cut off, Britain turned to India, and Indian raw cotton exports rose, pushing up prices for local weavers.

qa.q: In which year did the first cotton mill come up in Bombay?
qa.e: Bombay's first cotton mill came up in 1854. 1874 is Madras, 1912 is Tata steel and 1917 is Hukumchand's jute mill.

qa.q: Who set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in 1917?
qa.a: Seth Hukumchand
qa.e: Seth Hukumchand, a Marwari businessman, set up the first Indian-owned jute mill in Calcutta in 1917.

qa.q: Where did the Tata Iron and Steel works begin production in 1912?
qa.a: Jamshedpur
qa.e: The Tata Iron and Steel works began production at Jamshedpur in 1912. The town is named after Jamsetji Tata, who planned the steel works.

qa.q: Who was a jobber in Indian mills?
qa.a: A trusted worker who recruited people from villages for the mill
qa.e: Jobbers brought workers from their villages and helped them settle, but over time gained power and demanded gifts.

qa.q: How did the First World War help Indian industries?
qa.a: Manchester imports fell and Indian mills supplied war needs like uniforms and tents
qa.e: With British mills busy for the war, Indian mills gained the home market and army orders, and grew rapidly.

qa.q: What is the main aim of an advertisement?
qa.a: To make a product appear desirable and necessary
qa.e: Advertisements try to shape people's minds and create new needs so that buyers want the product.

qa.q: Why did Manchester industrialists print 'MADE IN MANCHESTER' on cloth labels?
qa.a: To make buyers confident about the quality of the cloth
qa.e: The place-name, printed in bold, told buyers the cloth came from a famous industrial centre, making them trust its quality.

qa.q: Why did some labels carry images of Indian gods and goddesses?
qa.a: To suggest divine approval and make the product feel familiar to buyers
qa.e: Images like Krishna or Saraswati made the foreign product seem trustworthy and familiar to Indian buyers.

qa.q: Why were calendars an effective way to advertise?
qa.a: They were used even by people who could not read and hung on walls all year
qa.e: Calendars stayed on walls in homes, tea shops and offices for a whole year, so people saw the product daily.

qa.q: Why were images of emperors and nawabs used in advertisements?
qa.a: To give the product a sense of respect and tradition
qa.e: Historical figures suggested that the product was as respected as royalty and connected to a proud past.

qa.q: What message did Indian manufacturers often put in their advertisements?
qa.a: If you care for the nation, buy products that Indians produce
qa.e: Indian advertisements carried the swadeshi idea, linking buying Indian goods with love for the nation.

qa.q: Where did printed calendars with product advertisements commonly hang?
qa.a: In tea shops, homes and offices
qa.e: Calendars were cheap and useful, so they were seen in everyday places by ordinary people.

qa.q: Which idea did advertisements by Indian manufacturers help spread?
qa.a: Swadeshi
qa.e: By urging people to buy Indian goods, advertisements became a vehicle of the swadeshi message.

qa.q: Which country developed the earliest kind of print technology?
qa.a: China
qa.e: China, along with Japan and Korea, had the earliest print technology, using hand printing from woodblocks.

qa.q: Why were traditional Chinese books folded into 'accordion books'?
qa.a: Only one side of the thin, porous paper could be printed
qa.e: Because both sides could not be printed, the printed sheets were folded and stitched at the side.

qa.q: What is the oldest Japanese book, printed in AD 868?
qa.a: The Buddhist Diamond Sutra
qa.e: The Diamond Sutra had six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations.

qa.q: Who brought the knowledge of woodblock printing from China to Italy?
qa.a: Marco Polo
qa.e: The explorer Marco Polo returned to Italy in 1295 with this knowledge.

qa.q: What was vellum?
qa.a: A parchment made from the skin of animals
qa.e: Vellum was used for luxury handwritten editions for aristocrats and rich libraries.

qa.q: Which of these experiences helped Gutenberg design his printing press?
qa.a: Seeing wine and olive presses on the estate where he grew up
qa.e: He adapted the idea of the screw press used for olives and grapes, and used his skill in making lead moulds for letters.

qa.q: About how many copies of the Bible did Gutenberg print, taking three years?
qa.e: About 180 copies were printed. Later, presses across Europe produced millions of books.

qa.q: What is meant by the 'print revolution'?
qa.a: The spread of printing that made books cheap and created a new reading public
qa.e: Between 1450 and 1550 presses spread across Europe, changing how people got information and knowledge.

qa.q: Who first brought the printing press to India?
qa.a: Portuguese missionaries in Goa
qa.e: The press came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid-16th century.

qa.q: By 1674, in which languages had about 50 books been printed by Jesuit priests?
qa.a: Konkani and Kannada
qa.e: Jesuit priests in Goa learnt Konkani and printed books in Konkani and Kannada.

qa.q: When and where was the first Tamil book printed?
qa.a: 1579, at Cochin
qa.e: Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book at Cochin in 1579.

qa.q: In which year was the first Malayalam book printed?
qa.e: The first Malayalam book was printed in 1713. By 1710 Dutch missionaries had printed 32 Tamil texts.

qa.q: By 1710, how many Tamil texts had Dutch Protestant missionaries printed?
qa.e: They printed 32 Tamil texts. About 50 books had been printed in Konkani and Kannada by 1674.

qa.q: Who began editing the Bengal Gazette in 1780?
qa.a: James Augustus Hickey
qa.e: Hickey's weekly was one of the earliest newspapers in India. Gangadhar Bhattacharya brought out the first Indian-run newspaper.

qa.q: Why did Warren Hastings persecute Hickey?
qa.a: Hickey published gossip about the Company's senior officials
qa.e: Hastings did not want Company officials criticised, so he persecuted Hickey and backed approved newspapers.

qa.q: Who was the first Indian to bring out a newspaper, the weekly Bengal Gazette?
qa.a: Gangadhar Bhattacharya
qa.e: Gangadhar Bhattacharya, who was close to Rammohun Roy, brought out the first Indian newspaper.

qa.q: Why was Erasmus worried about printing?
qa.a: He feared books would spread rebellious and irreligious ideas
qa.e: Erasmus, a Catholic reformer, felt that the flood of books could carry harmful ideas to readers.

qa.q: In which year did Martin Luther write the Ninety Five Theses?
qa.e: Luther wrote them in 1517. 1448 is Gutenberg's press, 1558 the Index of Prohibited Books and 1789 the French Revolution.

qa.q: What did Martin Luther's Ninety Five Theses criticise?
qa.a: Many practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church
qa.e: His criticism, spread through print, led to the Protestant Reformation.

qa.q: Which famous line about printing is linked with Martin Luther?
qa.a: Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one
qa.e: Luther praised print. Mercier called the press 'the most powerful engine of progress'.

qa.q: Why did the Roman Church start the Index of Prohibited Books from 1558?
qa.a: To control the spread of books it considered against its teachings
qa.e: Faced with new interpretations of faith spreading through print, the Church tried to ban certain books.

qa.q: What were chapbooks?
qa.a: Cheap pocket-sized books sold by pedlars in England
qa.e: Pedlars called chapmen sold chapbooks, so even the poor could buy something to read.

qa.q: Which is one way print is said to have helped the French Revolution?
qa.a: It popularised the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers like Voltaire and Rousseau
qa.e: Print spread Enlightenment ideas, built a culture of debate and mocked royalty, preparing the ground for revolution.

qa.q: Richard M. Hoe's power-driven cylindrical press could print how many sheets per hour?
qa.e: Hoe's press printed 8,000 sheets per hour, especially useful for newspapers.

qa.q: Which newspaper did Rammohun Roy publish from 1821?
qa.a: Sambad Kaumudi
qa.e: Rammohun Roy published the Sambad Kaumudi; the Samachar Chandrika was commissioned by orthodox groups to oppose his views.

qa.q: Which Gujarati newspaper was published in 1822?
qa.a: Bombay Samachar
qa.e: Bombay Samachar was the Gujarati paper of 1822. Jam-i-Jahan Nama and Shamsul Akhbar were Persian newspapers of the same year.

qa.q: What did the Deoband Seminary, founded in 1867, publish in large numbers?
qa.a: Fatwas guiding Muslims in their daily lives
qa.e: It published thousands of fatwas explaining the meaning of Islamic teachings for everyday life.

qa.q: Why was Rashsundari Debi's 'Amar Jiban' important?
qa.a: It was the first full-length autobiography in the Bengali language
qa.e: Published in 1876, it was written by a woman who had learnt to read secretly, showing how print gave women a voice.

qa.q: Which book did Jyotiba Phule write in 1871 about the injustices of the caste system?
qa.a: Gulamgiri
qa.e: In Gulamgiri, Phule wrote about caste injustice and linked it with the idea of slavery.

qa.q: Who wrote and published 'Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal' in 1938?
qa.a: Kashibaba, a Kanpur mill worker
qa.e: Kashibaba wrote about the links between caste and class exploitation, showing that workers too used print.

qa.q: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 was modelled on which laws?
qa.a: The Irish Press Laws
qa.e: It was modelled on the Irish Press Laws and gave the government wide powers to censor the vernacular press.

qa.q: Why was Bal Gangadhar Tilak imprisoned in 1908?
qa.a: He wrote with sympathy about deported Punjab revolutionaries in his paper Kesari
qa.e: His writing in Kesari about the revolutionaries deported in 1907 led to his imprisonment and widespread protests.
